content.title: Comparing Data Sets and Graphical Representations
content.overview: This lesson focuses on how to compare two or more data sets using measures of center (mean, median) and spread (range, standard deviation). On the SAT, you often need to determine the relative sizes of these statistics based on the shape of histograms, dot plots, or boxplots.
learning_objectives: Determine the relationship between the mean and median of different data sets based on graphical distributions.
Compare the standard deviations of different data sets by observing data volatility.
Analyze the impact of outliers on the mean and standard deviation.
Compare the centers of data sets using symmetry without performing specific calculations.

sections.title: Comparing Measures of Center: Mean vs. Median
sections.content: When comparing the centers of two data sets, first observe the symmetry of the distribution. For symmetric distributions, the mean is typically located at the center. If a distribution is right-skewed (long tail on the right), the mean is usually greater than the median; if it is left-skewed (long tail on the left), the mean is usually less than the median. When comparing two different symmetric distributions, the distribution where the data points are shifted further to the right has a larger mean and median.

sections.title: Comparing Spread: Standard Deviation and Range
sections.content:
Standard deviation measures the average distance of data points from the mean. The more spread out the data, the larger the standard deviation; the more concentrated the data is around the mean, the smaller the standard deviation. On the SAT, you do not need to calculate the exact standard deviation; you only need to compare it by observing the 'width' and 'density' of the graph. The range is the difference between the maximum and minimum values and is easily affected by extreme values.

![Comparison of Distributions with Different Spreads](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/365cdf51-57b6-4ecc-a4a1-20b4017397e0-1786502076707-829.webp)

sections.title: Relationship Between Graphical Features and Statistics
sections.content: The shapes of histograms and dot plots directly reflect statistical characteristics. If two data sets have the same range, but Data Set A is more concentrated in the middle while Data Set B is more distributed at the ends, then Data Set B has a larger standard deviation. Boxplots directly show the interquartile range (IQR) and range through the length of the box and the span of the whiskers.

worked_examples.question: Data Set A and Data Set B both contain 10 integers. The dot plot for Data Set A is uniformly distributed between 10 and 20. The dot plot for Data Set B has 5 dots at 10 and 5 dots at 20. Which data set has a larger standard deviation?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Analyze the distribution of the data. The data points in Data Set A are spread evenly between 10 and 20. Step 2: Analyze Data Set B; all points are located at the extreme ends (10 and 20), far from the center. Step 3: According to the definition of standard deviation, the further the data is from the center, the larger the standard deviation. Therefore, Data Set B has a larger standard deviation.

worked_examples.question: There are two symmetric histograms. The center of Histogram X is at 50, with a data range from 40 to 60. The center of Histogram Y is at 70, with a data range from 60 to 80. Compare their means.
worked_examples.solution: Since both histograms are symmetric, their means are equal to their center values. The mean of Histogram X is approximately 50, and the mean of Histogram Y is approximately 70. Therefore, the mean of Data Set Y is greater than the mean of Data Set X.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly assuming that the higher the bars in a histogram, the larger the standard deviation; in fact, standard deviation depends on the horizontal distribution of data along the x-axis, not the vertical frequency height.
Confusing range and standard deviation: range only looks at the two ends, while standard deviation looks at the distribution of all points relative to the center.
Ignoring outliers: outliers significantly pull the mean up or down but have a smaller impact on the median.
exam_tips: If two distributions have the exact same shape but different positions, their standard deviations are equal.
When comparing standard deviations, look for which graph has 'heavier tails' or more 'scattered' data.
For symmetric distributions, the mean equals the median; use this to quickly compare the centers of different symmetric graphs.
content.recap: When comparing data sets, determine the location of the mean by observing the balance point of the distribution, and determine the size of the standard deviation by observing the degree of clustering relative to the center. Symmetry is a key tool for simplifying comparisons.

knowledge_claims.content: For a symmetrically distributed data set, its mean and median are typically equal and located at the center of the distribution.
If two data sets have the exact same distribution shape but differ only in their position on the number line, their standard deviations are equal.
In a histogram, the further the data points are from the mean (i.e., the flatter the distribution or the more data at the ends), the larger the standard deviation.
In a histogram, the more concentrated the data points are near the mean (i.e., the sharper the distribution), the smaller the standard deviation.
The mean of a right-skewed distribution (long tail on the right) is typically greater than its median.
The mean of a left-skewed distribution (long tail on the left) is typically less than its median.
The range is determined solely by the difference between the maximum and minimum values and does not reflect the distribution of the data in between.
Standard deviation cannot be judged solely by the height of the bars in a histogram; the horizontal span and distribution must be considered.
When a very large outlier is added to a data set, the mean increases significantly, while the median may remain unchanged or change very little.
When comparing the means of two data sets, one can visually judge by finding the 'balance point' (center of gravity) of each graph.
